{{Short description|Number theory conjecture}}
In [[number theory]], the '''Agoh–Giuga conjecture''' on the [[Bernoulli number]]s <math>B_k</math> postulates that <math>p</math> is a [[prime number]] [[if and only if]] 

:<math>pB_{p-1} \equiv -1 \!\pmod p.</math> 

It is named after [[Takashi Agoh]] and [[Giuseppe Giuga]].

==Equivalent formulation==
The conjecture as stated above is due to Takashi Agoh;{{sfnp|Agoh|1995}} an equivalent formulation is due to Giuseppe Giuga, from 1950,{{sfnp|Giuga|1950}} to the effect that <math>p</math> is prime if and only if

:<math>1^{p-1}+2^{p-1}+ \cdots +(p-1)^{p-1} \equiv -1 \!\pmod p</math>,

which may also be written as

:<math>\sum_{i=1}^{p-1} i^{p-1} \equiv -1 \!\pmod p.</math>

It is trivial to show that <math>p</math> being prime is sufficient for the second equivalence to hold, since if <math>p</math> is prime, [[Fermat's little theorem]] states that

:<math>a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod p</math>

for <math>a = 1,2,\dots,p-1</math>, and the equivalence follows since <math>p-1 \equiv -1 \!\pmod p.</math>

==Status==
The statement is still a conjecture since it has not yet been proven that if a number <math>n</math> is not prime (that is, if <math>n</math> is [[composite number|composite]]), then the formula does not hold. It has been shown that a composite number <math>n</math> satisfies the formula if and only if it is both a [[Carmichael number]] and a [[Giuga number]], and that if such a number exists, it has at least 13,800 digits.{{sfnp|Borwein|Borwein|Borwein|Girgensohn|1996}} In 2001, Sorini showed that a possible counterexample should be greater than 10<sup>36067</sup>,{{sfnp|Sorini|2001}} which represents the limit suggested by Bedocchi for the demonstration technique specified by Giuga to his own conjecture.

==Relation to Wilson's theorem==
The Agoh–Giuga conjecture bears a similarity to [[Wilson's theorem]], which has been proven to be true. Wilson's theorem states that a number <math>p</math> is prime if and only if

:<math>(p-1)! \equiv -1 \!\pmod p,</math>

which may also be written as

:<math>\prod_{i=1}^{p-1} i \equiv -1 \!\pmod p.</math>

For an odd prime <math>p</math> we have

:<math>\prod_{i=1}^{p-1} i^{p-1} \equiv (-1)^{p-1} \equiv 1 \!\pmod p,</math>

and for <math>p=2</math> we have

:<math>\prod_{i=1}^{p-1} i^{p-1} \equiv (-1)^{p-1} \equiv 1 \!\pmod p.</math>

So, the truth of the Agoh–Giuga conjecture combined with Wilson's theorem gives: a number <math>p</math> is prime if and only if
 
:<math>\sum_{i=1}^{p-1} i^{p-1} \equiv -1 \!\pmod p</math>

and

:<math>\prod_{i=1}^{p-1} i^{p-1} \equiv 1 \!\pmod p.</math>
